parts: Cakes are made by creaming together fat and sugar, then adding eggs and flour, or by whisking eggs and sugar and then folding in flour. The outer layer or paste used to decorate a cake after baking is known as icing. Cakes are classified as cakes without icing (rich texture, higher percentage of fat, may contain dry fruits; eaten at high tea or as a snack, not as desserts: butter sponge, caramel cake, Madeira cake, Victoria sponge, Swiss roll) and cakes with icing (the base is a fatless sponge or genoese, e.g. cream and fruit cake, Black Forest cake, chocolate truffle cake, butter icing cake, royal icing cake). The four basic methods of cake making are: (1) rubbing-in method (chilled fat is rubbed into flour until it looks like bread crumbs; used when the weight of fat is not more than half that of flour), (2) creaming method (soft, not heated, fat is creamed with sugar until light and fluffy; used for richer cakes where fat and flour weights are equal), (3) whisking method (eggs and sugar are whisked to a thick foam and flour folded in; bake immediately or the batter will sink) and (4) all in one method (all ingredients are beaten together until smooth and creamy; used for quick preparation).

Check that ingredients and equipment are ready; weigh and measure carefully; follow the recipe exactly; use eggs and fat at room temperature; do not open the oven door unnecessarily; test for readiness (evenly browned, slightly away from the sides of the tin, springs back when pressed); cool slightly in the tin before turning out and let very rich cakes like wedding cakes cool completely in the tin. Preparing tins: baking sheets or trays for Swiss rolls and biscuits are greased; for rubbed-in cakes grease the tin and line the base with grease proof paper; for creamed mixtures line both sides and base with grease proof paper; for sponge cakes brush the tin with fat and coat with equal quantities of flour and caster sugar sifted together. A square tin holds the same amount of mixture as a round tin about 2 cm larger in diameter.
Cakes without icing and decorated cakes

Butter sponge is made by the creaming method; proper creaming is of utmost importance because the rise in volume depends on the air incorporated; variations are fruit cake (tutty fruity), Queen cake (raisins) and date and walnut cake. Caramel cake is darker and flavoured with caramel. Madeira cake has the sharp flavour of wine and a light taste of lemon, is coloured light yellow and is garnished with strips of orange peel. Victoria cake has flour, butter and sugar in equal proportion, is made by the all in one method and sandwiched with jam and sprinkled with icing sugar. Swiss roll is a rolled up cake whose base is a fatless sponge made by beating eggs, sugar and vanilla essence until very thick; the baked sponge is turned on butter paper, spread with jam and rolled while hot. Fatless sponge is the base of all decorated cakes; fatless chocolate cake replaces some flour with cocoa powder. Decorated cakes: cream and fruit cake (pineapple cake), Black Forest cake (chocolate sponge, cream icing, chocolate flakes and cherries), chocolate truffle cake, butter icing cake and royal icing cake (marzipan and royal icing).
Faults and remedies in cake baking

Cake faults are broadly divided into shape faults, structural faults, texture faults, crust faults, colour faults and miscellaneous faults. White spots on the surface: too much sugar, too little liquid, batter left standing before baking or very large sugar grains; use fine sugar and a balanced formula. Cake baked with peeled top: insufficient mixing or too much heat from the top (switch off the top element or cover the tin). Cake with flat top: oven too cool or incorrect balance between fat and egg. Under baked area under the crust: under baking or bumping the cake during baking. Heavy texture: too little baking powder, too much liquid or too little sugar. Cracks on the surface: too hot an oven, too little sugar or overfilling the tin. Discoloured crumb: too much bottom heat or too much baking powder. Mould growth: excessive moisture; do not wrap a cake while hot.
